paras: The Duval County polygamist shooting was the shooting of an unnamed Black man in Duval County, Florida, by a man described as a polygamist with three wives, reported in April 1882. The victim had been on his way to the court-house to file a complaint against the polygamist when he was overtaken and shot. The story survives only as a brief paragraph credited to the Chicago News that newspapers across the country reprinted as a curiosity.

According to the paragraph, a man living in Duval County had three wives, and a Black man "deemed it a duty to prosecute him." After gathering what the item called "the requisite proof," he set out for the court-house to make a complaint. He had gone only a few miles when "the polygamous husband overtook and shot him." The item gives no names, no date and no precise place, does not state the shooter's race, and does not say whether the victim died.
No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution of the shooter appears in the coverage.

The earliest copy found ran on April 12, 1882, without credit in a "Gleanings" column of the New Ulm Weekly Review in Minnesota, between a joke about swearing and a note on counterfeit coins. The next day the Highland Weekly News in Ohio printed it with a credit to the Chicago News, alongside items on Russian Jews in Syria and Mr. Vanderbilt's trotting horse. The same block of clipped items, with the same credit, appeared in the Iola Register in Kansas, the Republican in Maryland and the Grenada Sentinel in Mississippi within days.

A lightly reworded, uncredited version ran in the Douglas Independent in Oregon and later in the Vancouver Independent in Washington Territory. Louisiana papers carried it last, the Bossier Banner on May 4 and the Colfax Chronicle on May 6. Every version presented the shooting as an oddity of polygamy, called the victim "a negro," and offered no comment on the violence itself. No Florida report of the shooting was found.

framing.detail: Run without headline as a brief clipped item amid jokes and curiosities ('Gleanings'), calling the victim 'a negro' and treating polygamy as the point of interest.
